# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles WGS84 coordinates, occupational spans and benchmark population series for 159 excavated settlements across Upper Mississippi Hydrological Unit 07 (486.842 km²) from 9500BC to 1600AD [@kelly2025; @bird2022p3k14c].
Spanning Illinois (77 sites), Wisconsin (32), Minnesota (26), Iowa (13), Missouri (5), Indiana (5) and southwestern Michigan (1), the inventory tracks Early and Middle Archaic riverine base camps (Lang Farm, Apple Creek, Allen Fan, Buchanan and Koster), Middle Woodland Hopewell mound complexes (Albany Mounds, Kamp Mound, Elizabeth Mounds and Trempealeau), the Greater Cahokia urban hierarchy in the American Bottom (Cahokia, East St. Louis Mound Center, St. Louis Mound Group, Emerald Acropolis, Range Village Complex and Pulcher), Central Illinois Spoon River towns (Dickson Mounds, Orendorf and Larson), northern Mississippian-Oneota towns (Aztalan, Bryan Fortified Oneota Town, Silvernale, Bryan and Carcajou Point Oneota Town) and late precontact Oneota-Illinois centres (Zimmerman, Kathio, Oak Forest Longhouse Town, Moccasin Bluff Agricultural Town, Midway Village and Valley View) [@milner1998cahokia; @pauketat2004cahokia; @goldstein1991aztalan; @gibbon2012archaeology].
Synchronously active catalogued settlement totals peak at 33,76k in 1100AD (11,6% of the 290k HU 07 population), ease to 25,69k in 1200AD and 4,58k in 1500AD following the Vacant Quarter dispersal, and stand at 5,27k in 1600AD [@cobb2002vacant; @benson2009cahokia].
Source-ledger reconciliation confirms 159 included sites (502 benchmark observations, mean 3,16 per site, 123 carrying at least three benchmarks) and 170 excluded entries (167 duplicate-alias consolidations and 3 unquantified rockshelter exclusions), accounting for all 329 candidates with zero missing records.



# Background

Nucleated settlement in Upper Mississippi HU 07 evolved across four major archaeological phases [@theler2003driftless].
During the Early and Middle Archaic (9500BC to 3000BC), repeated occupations at deeply stratified terrace fans such as Apple Creek (260 peak, 8800BC to 1000AD), Napoleon Hollow (360 at 200AD, 5000BC to 900AD) and Koster (150 at 3000BC) anchored hunter-forager bands along the Illinois and Mississippi margins [@brown1983koster].
By 0AD to 400AD, Middle Woodland Havana-Hopewell societies built burial mound precincts and residential terraces at Albany Mounds (680 at 200AD), Kamp Mound (420 at 150AD) and Twenhafel (410 at 1000AD peak after long multi-component reuse).

Urbanisation culminated in the American Bottom during the Lohmann and Stirling phases (1050 to 1200AD), when Cahokia (18k at 1100AD), East St. Louis Mound Center (5,2k), St. Louis Mound Group (2,6k), Emerald Acropolis (1,6k), Range Village Complex (1,2k at 1050AD) and Pulcher (1,6k at 1150AD) formed an interconnected ceremonial and residential metropolis [@milner1998cahokia; @pauketat2004cahokia].
Northward Mississippian expansion reached Spoon River at Dickson Mounds (1,1k in 1200AD) and Orendorf (860 in 1220AD), the Crawfish River palisaded town of Aztalan (750 in 1100AD) and Red Wing locality towns at Silvernale (950 in 1150AD), Bryan (820 in 1200AD) and Bryan Fortified Oneota Town (950 in 1300AD) [@conrad1991middle; @goldstein1991aztalan; @gibbon2012archaeology].
After 1300AD, drought and conflict emptied the southern American Bottom during the Vacant Quarter abandonment, while Oneota, Langford and Illinois towns flourished at Zimmerman (1,8k in 1600AD), Carcajou Point Oneota Town (850 in 1350AD), Kathio (820 in 1600AD), Oak Forest Longhouse Town (800 in 1550AD), Moccasin Bluff Agricultural Town (700 in 1400AD), Carcajou Point (690 in 1500AD), Midway Village (640 in 1450AD) and Valley View (620 in 1550AD), paralleling contemporary Upper Mississippian centres along the Lake Michigan basin [@cobb2002vacant; @gibbon2012archaeology; @bettarel1973moccasin].

# Methodology

## Gazetteer Inclusion and Ledger Screening

All 329 candidate sites in the regional source ledger were screened against uniform gazetteer standards requiring surveyed WGS84 coordinates, dated residential or mound-precinct features and bounded phase population trajectories [@bird2022p3k14c; @kelly2025].
Where overlapping site reports fell within a 2 km radius of an existing canonical centre, duplicate entries were consolidated (167 duplicate-alias merges, including Mille Lacs-Kathio into Kathio, Bryan (Minnesota) into Bryan, Labras Lake into Range and Eveland into Dickson Mounds), alongside 3 unquantified non-habitation rockshelter exclusions (Lawrence I Rockshelter, Gottschall Rockshelter and Modoc Rockshelter), leaving 159 distinct entries in the regional settlement gazetteer.
All 159 retained records span 37,19 to 47,49 N and 86,36 to 96,75 W, comprise 502 dated observations (between two and nine benchmarks per site, averaging 3,16) and carry GMT+0 standardised timestamps.

## Household and Mound-Precinct Estimation

Mississippian town totals combine excavated wall-trench house densities, domestic precinct areas and contemporaneous occupation spans adjusted for timber-post replacement rates [@milner1998cahokia; @pauketat2004cahokia].
Archaic base-camp, Hopewell and Oneota estimates integrate stratified hearth counts, mapped residential terrace extents, storage-pit densities and burial-mound catchment populations [@brown1983koster; @theler2003driftless; @gibbon2012archaeology].

# Testing and Validation

Ledger checks confirm exact 159-to-159 parity between the source-ledger included set and the settlement gazetteer, plus 170 documented exclusions (167 duplicate-alias consolidations and 3 unquantified rockshelter exclusions; 329 candidates total, zero unaccounted rows).
Sub-regional coverage places 45 sites in the Upper Mississippi Headwaters, Minnesota River and Driftless Zone (15.820 peak sum), 59 in the Iowa-Des Moines, Rock and Upper Illinois Drift Plains (23.725 peak sum), and 55 in the American Bottom, Lower Illinois and Confluence (49.795 peak sum) (Table \ref{tab:um-subregion-summary}).
Chronological cross-checks capture the sequential regional shifts: Hopewellian Albany Mounds peaks in 200AD (680); the Greater Cahokia cluster peaks in 1050 to 1150AD (Cahokia 18k, East St. Louis Mound Center 5,2k, St. Louis Mound Group 2,6k, Emerald Acropolis 1,6k, Pulcher 1,6k, Range Village Complex 1,2k, alongside Aztalan 750); Spoon River towns peak in 1200 to 1250AD (Dickson Mounds 1,1k, Orendorf 860, Larson 720); and northern Oneota-Dakota-Illinois centres reach maximum scale in 1350 to 1600AD (Zimmerman 1,8k, Carcajou Point Oneota Town 850, Kathio 820, Oak Forest Longhouse Town 800) [@benson2009cahokia; @cobb2002vacant; @gibbon2012archaeology].

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Out of 159 catalogued settlements in the HU 07 gazetteer (whose individual peak populations sum to 89,34k), Table \ref{tab:gazetteer-upper-mississippi} presents the top 45 centres ranked by peak population descending, down to 480 inhabitants at Brems Yellow River Village.
Figure \ref{fig:settlements-upper-mississippi} displays the full rank-size distribution across all 159 settlements alongside the leading fifteen centres, anchored by Cahokia (18k), East St. Louis Mound Center (5,2k), St. Louis Mound Group (2,6k), Zimmerman (1,8k), Emerald Acropolis (1,6k), Pulcher (1,6k), Range Village Complex (1,2k) and Dickson Mounds (1,1k).

# Limitations

Three limitations affect site-level resolution in HU 07.
First, Greater Cahokia population estimates remain sensitive to assumed wall-trench house longevity and seasonal ceremonial aggregation versus year-round residency [@milner1998cahokia; @pauketat2004cahokia].
Second, Cahokia, East St. Louis Mound Center, St. Louis Mound Group, Pulcher and Apple Creek sit near the HU 07-HU 10 seam and require cross-unit deduplication prior to continental gazetteer harmonisation.
Third, nineteenth-century urban construction in St. Louis and East St. Louis, reservoir flooding and deep agricultural ploughing across the Illinois Valley truncated smaller mound peripheries and shallow floodplain hamlets.
